content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a common bacterial condition that can result in serious complications, such as urethral strictures, abscess formation, fistulas, bloodstream infections (bacteraemia), sepsis, kidney infections (pyelonephritis), and even kidney dysfunction. Mortality rates associated with UTIs can reach up to 1% in men and 3% in women, particularly when pyelonephritis develops. Probiotics, which are widely available without a prescription, have been proposed as a potential preventive therapy for UTIs. Evaluating their effectiveness could help both consumers and healthcare providers make informed decisions about their use as a prophylactic option. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether probiotics, in any formulation, provided a therapeutic advantage in reducing morbidity and mortality associated with UTIs when compared to placebo or no treatment. Additionally, the review sought to compare the efficacy of probiotics to other preventive measures, such as continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, topical estrogen, or cranberry juice, in populations susceptible to UTIs. To address these questions, a systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialized Register up to September 21, 2015. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving either individuals with a history of UTIs or healthy participants. These studies compared probiotics to placebo, no treatment, or other prophylactic interventions. The data were analyzed using a random-effects model, and the results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for binary outcomes. Nine studies involving a total of 735 participants were included in the review. Four studies compared probiotics to placebo, two compared probiotics to no treatment, two compared probiotics to antibiotics in patients with UTIs, and one study compared probiotics to placebo in healthy women. All studies aimed to assess differences in the rates of recurrent UTIs. However, the review identified significant limitations in the included studies, such as small sample sizes and insufficient methodological detail, which introduced a high risk of bias. This compromised the reliability of the findings and raised concerns that any reported treatment effects might be misleading or overestimated. The analysis found no significant reduction in the risk of recurrent symptomatic bacterial UTIs when comparing probiotics to placebo (six studies, 352 participants: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.12; I² = 23%). Similarly, no significant difference was observed between probiotics and antibiotics in reducing recurrent symptomatic bacterial UTIs (one study, 223 participants: RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.33). The confidence intervals were wide, and statistical heterogeneity was low. Adverse effects associated with probiotics were generally mild and included diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, and vaginal symptoms. None of the included studies reported data on asymptomatic bacterial UTIs, all-cause mortality, or cases of confirmed bacteraemia or fungaemia. Two studies documented participant withdrawal due to adverse events. In one study, 5.2% of participants in the probiotic group and 12.2% in the antibiotic group discontinued treatment due to adverse events. In another study, one participant in the placebo group withdrew for the same reason. The authors concluded that there was no significant benefit of probiotics compared to placebo or no treatment in preventing recurrent UTIs. However, due to the small number of studies, their limited sample sizes, and poor methodological quality, a potential benefit cannot be definitively ruled out. There was also limited information on the safety and mortality associated with probiotics, and no evidence was available regarding their impact on serious adverse events. Current evidence is insufficient to determine whether probiotics reduce or increase the risk of recurrent UTIs in women with a history of recurrent infections. Additionally, there was not enough evidence from a single RCT to draw conclusions about the comparative effectiveness of probiotics versus antibiotics.
